author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: If a man does not keep pace

why: The real 'different drummer': permission to be yourself, in an image everyone knows.

author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: If you have built castles in the air

why: A famous turn that rewards dreamers and then sets them to work.

author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: I learned this, at least, by my experiment

why: The true wording of the famous misquote; strong, but Thoreau already has two picks (2 per work).

author: Henry David Thoreau
location: Chapter 2, “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For”

span.from: Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in

why: Beautiful image; same chapter as starter #8, and the work cap is 2.

author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation

why: Famous but bleak on its own; better as a later 'deep' pick than a first impression.

author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: However mean your life is

why: Good steadying line; Thoreau's quota is taken.

author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: Only that day dawns to which we are awake

why: The book's last lines; lovely, held for a later batch.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself

why: Emerson's closing line: peace comes from within, then from principle.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: To be great is to be misunderstood

why: Famous, but alone it can sound self-flattering; the list before it carries the weight.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: Insist on yourself; never imitate

why: Short and true, but close to starter #1 in spirit.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: What I must do is all that concerns me

why: Solid, a little flat next to the others.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: A friend is a person with whom I may be sincere

why: The definition of a friend people quote at weddings and funerals.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: The only reward of virtue is virtue
span.to: to have a friend is to be one

why: Famous second half; Emerson is at his cap.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

span.from: Nothing great was ever achieved without

why: One of the most quoted lines in American prose, verified in its essay.

author: Marcus Aurelius

span.from: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years

why: Memento mori as a call to goodness, in three short sentences.

author: Marcus Aurelius

span.from: Look within. Within is the fountain of good

why: A clear image: goodness as a spring you keep digging for.

author: Marcus Aurelius

span.from: No longer talk at all about the kind of man

why: Long's real wording of 'Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be'; Marcus is at his cap.

author: Marcus Aurelius

span.from: Such as are thy habitual thoughts
span.to: the soul is dyed by the thoughts

why: Lovely 'dyed by the thoughts'; held for a later batch.

author: Marcus Aurelius

span.from: If it is not right, do not do it

why: Plain and strong; Marcus is at his cap.

author: Marcus Aurelius

span.from: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly
span.to: the work of a human being

why: The relatable 'getting out of bed' passage; held.

author: Epictetus

span.from: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish

why: The Stoic core in one sentence, with a real turn.

author: The Buddha

span.from: Hatred does not cease by hatred

why: One of the oldest moral sentences in the world, and still true.

author: The Buddha

span.from: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind

why: A steadying image for anyone facing criticism.

author: The Buddha

span.from: All that we are is the result of what we have thought
span.to: a shadow that never leaves him

why: Famous opening; the Buddha is capped at 2 per work and these two are stronger.

author: The Buddha

span.from: As rain does not break through a well-thatched house

why: Good image; held.

author: The Buddha

span.from: Wise people, after they have listened to the laws

why: Calm image, less famous.

author: Lao Tzu

span.from: He who knows other men is discerning
span.to: he who overcomes himself is mighty

why: The great self-knowledge chiasmus, in Legge's own wording.

author: Lao Tzu

span.from: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water

why: Water beats stone: strong, but Legge's syntax is heavy.

author: Confucius

span.from: Learning without thought is labour lost

why: A perfect antithesis, as true for a student as for a sage.

author: Confucius
location: Book XV (Wei Ling Kung), ch. XXIII

span.from: What you do not want done to yourself

why: The Golden Rule, five centuries before the Gospels.

author: Confucius

span.from: When we see men of worth

why: Good, but Confucius already has two.

author: Kahlil Gibran

span.from: Your children are not your children

why: Among the most loved passages in The Prophet; parents carry it for life.

author: Kahlil Gibran

span.from: The deeper that sorrow carves
span.to: the more joy you can contain

why: Consolation with a real turn: grief enlarges the heart.

author: Kahlil Gibran

span.from: You give but little when you give of

why: Famous; Gibran is capped at two from one work.

author: Kahlil Gibran

span.from: But let there be spaces in your

why: Wedding favourite; the 'But' needs the passage before it.

author: Kahlil Gibran

span.from: For what is it to die but to stand naked

why: Beautiful but about death: keep for a user who picks it, not a first batch.

author: Rabindranath Tagore

span.from: Let life be beautiful like summer flowers

why: Tagore's most quoted line; life and death in two images.

author: Rabindranath Tagore

span.from: Every child comes with the message

why: Hope in a single sentence; widely quoted.

author: Rabindranath Tagore

span.from: Clouds come floating into my life

why: Lovely; Tagore capped at two from Stray Birds.

author: Rabindranath Tagore

span.from: The bird wishes it were a cloud

why: Playful mirror; light charge.

author: Rabindranath Tagore

span.from: We read the world wrong

why: Sharp but abstract.

author: Michel de Montaigne
location: Essays, Book II, ch. XII, “Apology for Raimond Sebond”

span.from: When I play with my cat

why: Delight and humility in one line; the cat line people love.

author: Michel de Montaigne
location: Essays, Book I, ch. XXV, “Of the Education of Children”

span.from: The most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness

why: Warm, a little plain.

author: Leo Tolstoy
location: Book Twelve, Chapter XVI, Prince Andrew

span.from: Love hinders death. Love is life

speaker: Prince Andrew
why: Prince Andrew's insight as he nears death: love as the only key.

author: George Eliot

span.from: the growing good of the world is partly

why: The great last sentence of Middlemarch: quiet lives matter.

author: George Eliot

span.from: If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life

why: Breathtaking, but long and needs its paragraph.

author: Charlotte Brontë

span.from: Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little

speaker: Jane
why: Jane's great claim to an equal soul; next to starter #13 but its own moment.

author: Charlotte Brontë

span.from: Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity

speaker: Helen Burns
why: Helen Burns on forgiveness: short, wise and freeing.

author: Charlotte Brontë

span.from: I care for myself. The more
span.to: the more I will respect myself

speaker: Jane
why: Powerful; Brontë has two already.

author: L. M. Montgomery

span.from: I’m so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers

speaker: Anne
why: Pure delight, and a line readers love every autumn.

author: L. M. Montgomery

span.from: Kindred spirits are not so scarce as I used to think
span.to: so many of them in the world

speaker: Anne
why: Sweet; Montgomery has one.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

span.from: even if the doctor does not give you a year

why: Courage at the edge of life: make one brave push.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

span.from: Extreme busyness

why: Witty; a little arch.

author: Booker T. Washington

span.from: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour

why: Refusing hate as self-respect: one of the strongest lines in the book.

author: Booker T. Washington
location: Chapter XIV, the Atlanta Exposition address

span.from: No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much

why: Good, but speaks to a group more than a reader.

author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
location: “Sympathy”, stanza 3, last 4 lines (Lyrics of the Hearthside, 1899)

span.from: It is not a carol of joy or glee
span.to: I know why the caged bird sings

why: The line Maya Angelou took her title from; it carries the whole poem.

author: Paul Laurence Dunbar

span.from: We wear the mask that grins and lies

why: A great poem of hidden pain, still painfully current.

author: Walt Whitman
location: “O Me! O Life!” (Leaves of Grass, 1891–92), the answer

span.from: That you are here

why: The answer to 'O me! O life!': you may contribute a verse.

author: Walt Whitman

span.from: Afoot and light-hearted I take to the open road

why: Joyful opening; Whitman has one.

author: William Wordsworth
location: “I wandered lonely as a Cloud”, last stanza

span.from: For oft, when on my couch I lie

why: The daffodils that 'flash upon that inward eye': memory as solace.

author: William Wordsworth

span.from: What though the radiance which was once so bright

why: 'Splendour in the grass': the great consolation for lost youth.

author: Christina Rossetti

span.from: Does the road wind up-hill all the way
span.to: From morn to night, my friend

why: A small dialogue about a long road; honest and kind.

author: Christina Rossetti

span.from: Better by far you should forget and smile

why: Beautiful; grief-adjacent, offer when chosen.

author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

span.from: In the Spring a young man’s fancy

why: Famous and light; speaker's mood sours later.

author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

span.from: If thou must love me, let it be for nought

why: Love for its own sake; a second sonnet alongside starter #25.

author: Socrates
location: Apology 42a, Socrates’ last words to the jury

span.from: The hour of departure has arrived

why: Socrates' last words at his trial, calm before death.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

span.from: Lives of great men all remind us
span.to: Footprints on the sands of time

why: 'Footprints on the sands of time': the stanza everyone remembers.

author: John Donne

span.from: any man’s death diminishes me

why: 'For whom the bell tolls': the second half of starter #60's passage.

author: William Blake
location: Auguries of Innocence, lines 55–59 (Pickering Manuscript, unpunctuated)

span.from: Man was made for Joy

why: Joy and woe woven together: consolation without denial.

author: William Ernest Henley

span.from: Out of the night that covers me

why: Invictus's first stanza; the starter already has its last.

author: Mary Shelley

span.from: Nothing is so painful to the human mind as a great and sudden change

speaker: Victor
why: True but flat on its own.

author: Lewis Carroll

span.from: It’s a poor sort of memory that only works backwards

speaker: the White Queen
why: Carroll's delight: a joke that is also a thought.

author: Mark Twain

span.from: Let us endeavor so to live that when we come to die

why: Twain's best Calendar line: a joke with a moral.

author: Mary Wollstonecraft

span.from: It is justice, not charity, that is wanting in the world

why: Seven words that still sharpen every argument about fairness.

author: John Muir

span.from: Another glorious Sierra day

why: Joyful; Muir's lines from Our National Parks are stronger.

author: Okakura Kakuzō

span.from: The art of life lies in a constant readjustment

why: A quietly wise definition of living well.

author: Ohiyesa (Charles Eastman)
location: Chapter IV, “Barbarism and the Moral Code”

span.from: Silence is the absolute poise or balance

why: Next to starter #59 in the same paragraph.

author: Jane Austen

span.from: Till this moment I never knew myself

speaker: Elizabeth
why: Needs the letter scene.

author: Sara Teasdale

span.from: Spend all you have for loveliness
span.to: Count many a year of strife well lost

why: The stanza that turns Barter into a call to live.

author: Louisa May Alcott

span.from: Love is the only thing that we can carry with us

speaker: Beth
why: Beth's farewell: moving but tied to her death.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett

span.from: Where you tend a rose, my lad

why: A small verse with a true idea: tend good thoughts.

author: Virginia Woolf

span.from: She had a perpetual sense
span.to: far out to sea and alone

why: Beautiful prose, needs the scene.
